title: Instability as Signal: Diagnosing Latent Heterogeneity in Multimodal Survival Models
abstract: Multimodal deep learning models for cancer survival prediction frequently exhibit unstable and irreproducible performance, limiting their clinical applicability. Rather than proposing a new predictive architecture, this work presents a diagnostic investigation into the sources of this instability. Using a transformer-based deep fusion model combining RNA sequencing and histopathology data from the TCGA-BRCA cohort as a diagnostic probe, we demonstrate that global survival prediction is highly unstable across data splits. We then analyze the learned multimodal embeddings in an unsupervised manner, revealing stable latent patient subgroups with significantly divergent survival outcomes. These subgroups are not explained by canonical receptor status or immune infiltration, but instead align with tumor-intrinsic proliferative activity. Conditioning survival modeling on the largest discovered subgroup recovers strong and stable prognostic performance, substantially outperforming unimodal baselines. These findings indicate that survival predictability is conditional on latent heterogeneity and suggest that heterogeneity-aware modeling strategies are essential for robust multimodal prognostication. This work establishes a methodological framework for interpreting instability in multimodal survival learning.
authorString: Ray R, Shekhawat SS.

title: CytoLens: a modular deep learning system for quantitative cervical cytology
abstract: Cervical cytology screening relies on the visual assessment of nuclear and cellular morphology across thousands of cells per slide, a labor-intensive task that could benefit from quantitative computational support. Here we present CytoLens, a modular deep learning system that detects and counts nuclei, delineates nuclei and whole cells, measures the nuclear-to-cell area ratio (N:C), classifies cells from multifocal images and scores candidate abnormality. We trained and tested each module on a public dataset matched to its task, without pooling datasets. CytoLens detected nuclei with an F1 score of 0.931 (95% confidence interval (CI), 0.914–0.946) and counted 75 of 100 fields to within one nucleus. Point-prompted segmentation achieved mean Dice coefficients of 0.901 for nuclei and 0.847 for whole cells and, without retraining, transferred to a second dataset in which measured N:C increased with lesion grade in parallel with expert outlines. Multifocal hierarchical classification reached a mean accuracy of 0.947 across four Bethesda-aligned categories, and abnormality scores ranked annotated abnormal candidates with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.865. These results support the evaluation of CytoLens on patient-linked clinical specimens.
authorString: Lee K, Yoon RJ, Lee RS, Lee D.

title: CytoRipple: Mapping Tissue Polarization through Subcellular Cytoskeleton Dynamics
abstract: Spatial multi-omic technologies entail simultaneous measurement of tens-to-thousands of molecular features (e.g. RNA, protein). While cell type and state profiling is the major focus of spatial multi-omic analyses, cytoskeletal proteins are often solely utilized for cell segmentation and quality control. Here, we introduce a new computational framework, CytoRipple, that leverages these concomitant spatially-resolved single-cell measurements of cytoskeleton proteins to identify tissue-level vector fields. Polarization vectors are known to associate with cell movement and phenotype, inferring their physical orientation. We validate these associations across biological contexts and reveal how polarization vector fields can be harnessed to discover multi-cellular structures (e.g. “streams” of cells with similar polarizations). These multi-cellular cytoskeleton dynamics associate with distinct phenomena, such as vector “divergence” with CD8 + T cell activation and “streams” with spatially segmented stages of the anti-tumor immune response. Together, these data support a role for CytoRipple in revealing a dynamic layer across spatial multi-omic platforms.

title: Preoperative thymic output and T-cell repertoire diversity are associated with recurrence after nephrectomy for localized renal cell carcinoma
abstract: Radiographic thymic health and peripheral T-cell repertoire features have been linked to outcomes in renal cell carcinoma (RCC), but their prognostic value after curative-intent surgery is unclear. We quantified preoperative blood signal-joint T-cell receptor excision circles (sjTRECs), a marker of thymic output, in 218 patients with localized RCC undergoing nephrectomy and characterized T-cell receptor β (TCRβ) repertoires in 201 patients. We assessed overall survival (OS) and recurrence-free survival (RFS) using Kaplan-Meier and Cox models adjusted for age, sex, and Leibovich risk group. High sjTREC levels were associated with longer RFS after adjustment for age, sex, and Leibovich risk group (hazard ratio [HR] 0.50; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.29-0.87; p=0.015), with a concordant OS estimate (HR 0.62; 95% CI, 0.38-1.02; p=0.058). sjTREC provided additional prognostic information beyond Leibovich risk stratification for recurrence overall and among intermediate/high-risk patients (likelihood-ratio test, p=0.024 and p=0.034, respectively). Higher TCRβ diversity was associated with longer RFS overall (HR 0.76; 95% CI, 0.60-0.96; p=0.024) and among intermediate/high-risk patients with longer RFS (HR 0.71; 95% CI, 0.55-0.92; p=0.009) and OS (HR 0.80; 95% CI, 0.65-0.98; p=0.031). Preoperative sjTREC provided prognostic information beyond clinicopathological risk, with higher TCRβ diversity associated with favorable outcomes.

title: LightSuite: scalable atlas registration and cell detection across the central nervous system
abstract: ABSTRACT Deciphering brain-wide circuits requires large animal cohorts, yet computational bottlenecks in atlas registration and whole-volume cell detection reduce precision, reproducibility, and sample yield. We present LightSuite, an open-source framework enabling scalable, multimodal registration and cellular mapping across the central nervous system (CNS). LightSuite combines damage-resilient 3D point-cloud initialization with user-steerable non-rigid registration, and GPU-accelerated local background normalization for rapid, illumination-invariant cell detection. Applying LightSuite to Fos-dependent activity labeling in mice, we extracted reproducible, layer-resolved profiles of active cell density, soma-size distributions and per-animal labeling-efficiency factors. LightSuite computationally untwists and registers cleared spinal cords to map myeloarchitecture, reconstructs serial wide-field histology to map surface GluA1 distributions, resolves optic fiber tracks, and aligns in vivo functional ultrasound hemodynamics into common atlas coordinates. LightSuite establishes an integrated, accessible platform for cohort-level structural, molecular, and functional CNS mapping.

title: Childhood Trauma and Cortical Thickness in Bipolar Disorder with and without Psychosis: Effects by Diagnostic Group and Trauma Subtype
abstract: Abstract Background Bipolar disorder affects about 2-3% of the population and is associated with cortical abnormalities, with bipolar disorder with psychosis (BDP) reported to show more pronounced changes. It remains unclear whether childhood trauma is associated with cortical thickness differences across bipolar disorder subgroups, particularly in BDP. Methods Using the publicly available PARDIP (Psychosis and Affective Research Domains and Intermediate Phenotypes) data set, we examined whether childhood trauma was associated with cortical thickness differences among 120 individuals: 33 with bipolar disorder without psychosis (BD; 36% male), 38 with bipolar disorder with psychosis (BDP; 47% male), and 49 healthy controls (HC; 61% male). Participants completed the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire-Short Form (CTQ-SF), and T1-weighted MRI scans were processed with FreeSurfer to extract cortical thickness across the 68 Desikan-Killiany regions. Linear mixed effects models tested associations between CTQ subtype scores and cortical thickness and trauma-by-diagnosis interactions, with sensitivity analyses for medication class and illness duration following the ENIGMA guidelines. Results No cortical thickness difference survived correction for multiple testing. At the nominal level, BD showed reduced thickness relative to HC in cingulate, frontal and occipital regions, whereas BDP showed greater superior temporal thickness relative to BD. Sexual abuse was nominally associated with reduced temporal thickness. Exploratory trauma-by-diagnosis interactions suggested region- and subtype-specific patterns that did not survive correction. Medication class and illness duration showed no significant effects after FDR correction. Conclusions These exploratory findings suggest nominal, region-specific associations between childhood trauma subtypes and cortical thickness in bipolar disorder. However, no findings survived correction for multiple comparisons, so they should be read as preliminary and need replication in larger samples.

title: PIEZO1 mediates mechanosensing and myofibroblastic activation of synovial fibroblasts in post-traumatic osteoarthritis
abstract: Fibrosis and inflammation of the synovium are common pathological features of joint diseases. In osteoarthritis (OA), extensive evidence supports that synovial pathology drives symptoms and disease progression, yet the mechanisms underpinning pathological synovial remodeling, including fibrosis, remain unclear. Here, we identify the mechanosensitive ion channel PIEZO1 as a critical regulator of myofibroblast-like activation of synovial fibroblasts (SFs) in post-traumatic osteoarthritis (PTOA). Using multi-omic assessments in human and murine synovium, a murine model of joint injury, histopathology, and functional in vitro phenotyping, we demonstrate that joint injury triggers expansion of myofibroblast-like SFs concurrent with fibrotic remodeling and mechanical stiffening of the synovium. Myofibroblastic commitment of synovial progenitors was associated with activation of the YAP1 regulon, and PIEZO1 agonism drove nuclear accumulation of YAP1 in SFs. PIEZO1 was enriched in synovia of injured joints, and in cultured SFs pharmacologic PIEZO1 activation promoted αSMA enrichment and increased matrix contraction, which were both ablated by YAP1 inhibition. PIEZO1 silencing abrogated TGF-β-induced contractility and markedly altered the transcriptomic response to mechanical loading in vitro , including ECM production and neuroinflammatory programs. In vivo , acute intra-articular pharmacologic PIEZO1 activation induced a pro-fibrotic, pro-inflammatory, and anti-adipogenic transcriptomic program in synovium. Collectively, these findings establish PIEZO1 as a key mediator of the pathogenic activation of SFs and identify aberrant mechanosensing as a mechanism underlying synovial fibrosis in PTOA.

title: Optimising neural contrast and minimising tissue shrinkage in dragon lizard brains: buffered Lugol’s iodine versus phosphotungstic acid for contrast-enhanced µCT
abstract: Contrast-enhanced micro-computed tomography (µCT) has become a valuable tool for addressing neuroanatomical questions that previously required destructive histology. As a relatively new technique, it remains subject to ongoing technical refinement, and taxon- and tissue-specific protocol optimisation. We evaluated the performance of two common contrast-enhancing agents, buffered Lugol’s iodine and phosphotungstic acid (PTA) in aqueous solution, for µCT visualisation of the nervous system in the Jacky dragon lizard, Amphibolurus muricatus by comparing staining time, contrast specificity and brain tissue shrinkage evaluated at three concentrations (1.25%, 2.5% and 5%). Buffered Lugol’s iodine outperformed aqueous PTA by requiring shorter staining times (as short as four days) and providing better white matter-grey matter differentiation, whereas PTA required longer incubation periods of approximately three weeks and produced poorer white-grey matter differentiation. Importantly, buffered Lugol’s iodine produced higher brain-to-endocast occupancy estimates than aqueous PTA, suggesting substantially reduced tissue shrinkage. PTA-treated specimens exhibited an estimated 13.3% reduction in occupancy and approximately 20% greater brain tissue shrinkage than buffered Lugol’s-treated specimens. Together, these findings demonstrate that buffered Lugol’s iodine staining provides the high level of internal tissue contrast required to resolve fine-scale neuroanatomical organisation in three dimensions, preserves the spatial relationships among anatomical structures, and reduces artefacts, all of which result in a closer correspondence between the brain and endocranial cavity. From a practical perspective, the study provides guidance for contrast agent selection in future µCT studies and reveals that buffered Lugol’s iodine is better suited to fine-scale neuroanatomical, volumetric and geometric morphometric analyses, whereas PTA is advantageous for applications prioritising general soft-tissue or musculoskeletal visualisation. title: Tracheal Eccentricity is Associated with Respiratory Morbidity and Mortality in Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease
abstract: Background Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is characterized by airway remodeling, which may affect tracheal morphology. However, the relationship between tracheal morphometry and COPD severity, quality of life, functional capacity, and mortality remains poorly understood. Objective To investigate the associations between CT-derived tracheal lumen eccentricity and clinical outcomes in COPD. Methods We analyzed data from 8,383 participants in the multicenter COPDGene study. Tracheal lumen eccentricity (ε) was calculated at each cross-section using the major and minor axes lengths and deriving final value using the arithmetic mean across all tracheal slices, where ε = 0 represents a circle and ε > 0 indicates an ellipse. Baseline assessments included spirometry measurements, 6-minute walk distance (6MWD), St. George’s Respiratory Questionnaire (SGRQ), and the modified Medical Research Council (mMRC) dyspnea score. Longitudinal assessments included annualized lung function change and all-cause mortality. Multivariable models were used to evaluate associations between tracheal eccentricity and clinical outcomes. Results Tracheal eccentricity increased with severity of airflow obstruction (0.60±0.07, 0.61±0.07, 0.62±0.07, 0.64±0.08, and 0.64±0.08 in GOLD stages 0 through 4, respectively). Higher tracheal eccentricity was independently associated with lower FEV 1 (β = −0.30 L, 95% CI: −0.47 to −0.14, p<0.001), lower FEV 1 /FVC (β = −0.06, 95% CI: −0.09 to −0.04, p<0.001), lower 6MWD (β = −15.7 m, 95% CI: −25.2 to −6.2, p=0.001), higher SGRQ score (β = 16.9, 95% CI: 11.2 to 22.5, p<0.001), higher mMRC dyspnea score (β = 0.4, 95% CI: 0.1 to 0.6, p=0.007), and accelerated lung function decline (β = −23.8 ml/year, 95% CI: −2.48 to −45.13, p=0.029). Increased tracheal eccentricity is associated with increased all-cause mortality (adjusted HR: 1.81 [95% CI, 1.01-3.26]; p = 0.047). Conclusions These findings suggest that tracheal morphology may serve as an imaging biomarker for COPD outcomes, supported by significant associations with lower quality of life, lung function decline, and all-cause mortality.

title: Self-supervised pretraining for dermoscopic lesion segmentation with limited labels: A controlled comparison of initialisation strategies
abstract: Background Self-supervised learning may improve segmentation when labelled data are limited, but its benefit may depend on model and initialisation strategy. This study evaluated in-domain masked-reconstruction pretraining across limited annotation budgets. Methods The International Skin Imaging Collaboration (ISIC) 2016 development set was partitioned into 765 images for self-supervised pretraining, 94 for fine-tuning and 41 for validation. Five nested annotation budgets (12–94 images) and five seeds were evaluated on the 379-image test set. A custom U-Net compared random and in-domain self-supervised initialisation; a ResNet-34 U-Net compared random, ImageNet, in-domain self-supervised and sequential ImageNet-to-self-supervised initialisation. Models trained with 94 labelled images were evaluated without adaptation on ISIC 2017. A separate experiment examined restoration-based pretraining. Results In the custom U-Net, self-supervised pretraining achieved higher mean Dice than random initialisation at all five budgets, including 0.664 versus 0.615 with 12 labels and 0.811 versus 0.768 with 94 labels. Seed-level 95% confidence intervals for paired differences excluded zero at 47 and 94 labels but not at the other budgets. With 47 labels, the self-supervised model achieved mean Dice of 0.789, compared with 0.768 for random initialisation with 94 labels. In ResNet-34, ImageNet initialisation achieved higher mean Dice than in-domain self-supervised pretraining at all five budgets, and adding self-supervised pretraining after ImageNet reduced mean Dice at four of five budgets. All six 94-label configurations achieved lower mean Dice on ISIC 2017 than ISIC 2016. In the restoration experiment, mean Dice was 0.686 with random initialisation and 0.638–0.642 following pretraining. Conclusions In-domain masked-reconstruction pretraining improved mean Dice relative to random initialisation in the custom U-Net, but not consistently in the ResNet-34 U-Net, where ImageNet initialisation performed better at every budget. Adding self-supervised pretraining after ImageNet provided no consistent gain. These findings are specific to the dermoscopic lesion-segmentation experiments and do not establish melanoma-specific diagnostic or clinical performance.

title: APOE ε4 Modifies the Association of Left Atrial Remodeling With Brain Aging
abstract: INTRODUCTION Whether APOE ε4 modifies relationships between subclinical cardiac phenotypes and brain structure is unknown. METHODS In Framingham Heart Study Offspring participants, we related antecedent echocardiographic remodeling (Examinations 4–6) to repeated brain MRI, and cardiac magnetic resonance phenotypes to regional cortical morphometry, testing cardiac × APOE ε4 interactions with false-discovery-rate (FDR) correction and permutation testing of the regional screen. RESULTS APOE ε4 modified the association between antecedent left atrial (LA) remodeling and subsequent lateral ventricular expansion (β=−0.00858, P=1.45×10⁻⁴, q=0.0023; N=1,305; 3,787 MRI observations), the only FDR-significant result of 16 longitudinal tests, including with participant-specific MRI-time slopes (q=0.034); it weakened when intracranial volume × MRI time was modeled. Four regional ventricular cardiac × APOE ε4 interactions met within-family FDR criteria, but their number was consistent with chance (permutation P=0.70). Maximum LA volume index showed an APOE ε4-dependent association with left middle-occipital cortical-thickness variability (whole-brain q=0.017; permutation P=0.041) that persisted after ventricular adjustment. Cardiac phenotypes and trajectories showed no FDR-significant APOE ε4-dependent associations with plasma Aβ42/40, p-tau181, GFAP, or NfL, and adjustment for these biomarkers changed the regional interactions by at most 3.2%. Allen Human Brain Atlas data showed cholesterol-biosynthesis enrichment in the right superior frontal cortex, implicated by the LV end-systolic volume interaction, but without convergent pathway evidence. DISCUSSION APOE ε4 modified atrial–brain relationships, with the strongest evidence linking antecedent atrial remodeling to later ventricular expansion. Replication with prespecified models is needed. Highlights APOE ε4 modified how left atrial remodeling related to later brain ventricle growth. It was the only FDR-significant result of 16 tests and persisted with random slopes. In ε4 carriers, larger LA volume tracked lower occipital thickness variability. This atrial–cortical association was independent of LV mass and ejection fraction. Exploratory: HbA1c related to LV end-diastolic volume differently by APOE ε4 status.
originalAbstract:
INTRODUCTION

Whether APOE ε4 modifies relationships between subclinical cardiac phenotypes and brain structure is unknown.

METHODS

In Framingham Heart Study Offspring participants, we related antecedent echocardiographic remodeling (Examinations 4–6) to repeated brain MRI, and cardiac magnetic resonance phenotypes to regional cortical morphometry, testing cardiac × APOE ε4 interactions with false-discovery-rate (FDR) correction and permutation testing of the regional screen.

RESULTS

APOE ε4 modified the association between antecedent left atrial (LA) remodeling and subsequent lateral ventricular expansion (β=−0.00858, P=1.45×10⁻⁴, q=0.0023; N=1,305; 3,787 MRI observations), the only FDR-significant result of 16 longitudinal tests, including with participant-specific MRI-time slopes (q=0.034); it weakened when intracranial volume × MRI time was modeled. Four regional ventricular cardiac × APOE ε4 interactions met within-family FDR criteria, but their number was consistent with chance (permutation P=0.70). Maximum LA volume index showed an APOE ε4-dependent association with left middle-occipital cortical-thickness variability (whole-brain q=0.017; permutation P=0.041) that persisted after ventricular adjustment. Cardiac phenotypes and trajectories showed no FDR-significant APOE ε4-dependent associations with plasma Aβ42/40, p-tau181, GFAP, or NfL, and adjustment for these biomarkers changed the regional interactions by at most 3.2%. Allen Human Brain Atlas data showed cholesterol-biosynthesis enrichment in the right superior frontal cortex, implicated by the LV end-systolic volume interaction, but without convergent pathway evidence.

DISCUSSION

APOE ε4 modified atrial–brain relationships, with the strongest evidence linking antecedent atrial remodeling to later ventricular expansion. Replication with prespecified models is needed.

Highlights

APOE ε4 modified how left atrial remodeling related to later brain ventricle growth. It was the only FDR-significant result of 16 tests and persisted with random slopes. In ε4 carriers, larger LA volume tracked lower occipital thickness variability. This atrial–cortical association was independent of LV mass and ejection fraction. Exploratory: HbA1c related to LV end-diastolic volume differently by APOE ε4 status.

title: MRI-Trackable Mesenchymal Stem Cells for Oncolytic Therapy: A Clinically Feasible Dual-Labeling Protocol
abstract: Non-invasive imaging of oncolytic virus-loaded mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) could help evaluate cell trafficking and delivery in cancer therapy. Labeling MSCs with iron oxide particles (IOPs) enables in vivo tracking using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). This study evaluated a dual-labeling strategy that loads MSCs with MegaPro IOPs and the oncolytic virus Delta-24-RGD (DNX-2401; tasadenoturev) and assessed cellular function and MRI detectability. MSCs were labeled with IOPs alone or in combination with the oncolytic virus. We compared cell viability and intracellular iron content among IOP-labeled, dual-labeled, and naïve MSCs, and evaluated differentiation, invasion, and immunophenotype in naïve and IOP-labeled MSCs. We evaluated phantoms containing varying numbers of IOP-labeled MSCs (9 × 10³–1.5 × 10 5 cells) using R2-, R2*-, and R1-weighted MRI, and generated corresponding relaxation rate maps to assess concentration dependent contrast and detection sensitivity. Iron content was comparable between IOP-labeled and dual-labeled MSCs (9.2 ± 2.6 and 11.6 ± 1.4 pg/cell, respectively), with >91% viability across all groups. IOP-labeled MSCs retained invasion and differentiation potential. At the highest labeled-cell concentration, R2*, R2, and R1 increased approximately 4, 2.5, and 1.5 fold, respectively, relative to the agarose control. The estimated detection limits were approximately 2 × 10³ cells for R2* and 6 × 10³ cells for R2 and R1. These findings demonstrate that dual labeling of MSCs with IOPs and oncolytic virus preserves key cellular characteristics while providing MRI-detectable contrast, supporting further investigation of this approach for image-guided tracking of cell-based cancer therapies.

title: Facilitating Valid Statistical Inference in Biomedical Image Synthesis
abstract: Generative AI for medical image synthesis is increasingly used to impute missing data and augment biomedical datasets. Yet despite achieving high computational similarity to their real-world counterparts, synthetic images remain uncommon in clinical research practice, in part because of concerns about their biological validity. Here, we evaluate whether synthetic images support reliable downstream statistical analysis and biological inference in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and multiplexed immunofluorescence (mIF) imaging. We find that associations between patient phenotypes and synthesized images can be severely attenuated. This is because synthesis methods typically omit clinically relevant covariates and therefore generate images that, although visually realistic, mask key biological differences. Furthermore, naive analyses treat synthesized images as if they were observed, ignoring the statistical uncertainty introduced by synthesis. Drawing on multiple imputation theory, we introduce Phenotype Aware Multiple Synthesis (PAMS), an analysis framework that requires no model retraining and instead adjusts synthesized output to recover valid biological estimates with appropriately calibrated uncertainty. Applied to MRI and mIF data, PAMS reduced estimation bias and restored nominal confidence interval coverage. Because it is compatible with existing synthesis pipelines, PAMS offers a practical and rigorous route to statistically and biologically valid use of synthesized images in biomedical imaging research.

title: Pharmacologic inhibition of OLIG2 by CT-179 disrupts mitotic progression and enhances standard-of-care chemoradiotherapy in glioblastoma
abstract: Background Glioblastoma (GBM) remains uniformly fatal. The basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor OLIG2 is universally expressed in diffuse glioma, sustains the tumor-propagating stem-like fraction, and opposes p53-mediated genotoxic responses, but has historically been considered undruggable. We characterized CT-179, a brain-penetrant small-molecule OLIG2 inhibitor, as a candidate therapeutic for GBM. Methods Target engagement was assessed by cellular thermal shift assay, differential scanning fluorimetry, crosslinking, and electrophoretic mobility shift assay. Anti-tumor activity was evaluated across eleven patient-derived GBM cell lines, in zebrafish oligodendrocyte precursor cell (OPC)-derived tumors, and orthotopic and subcutaneous GBM models, including combinations with radiotherapy plus temozolomide and with selective Bcl-2 family inhibitors. Results: : CT-179 engaged OLIG2 and altered the conformation of dimerized OLIG2 on chromatin without preventing dimerization or fully displacing OLIG2 from DNA. CT-179 reduced OLIG2-positive OPC’s and OPC-derived tumors in zebrafish and inhibited proliferation across all eleven GBM lines (IC50 < 360 nM), depleting the stem-like fraction and inducing apoptosis through mitotic catastrophe, mitotic slippage, or a hybrid response. RNA-seq across three patient-derived glioma stem cell lines identified β-tubulin gene isoforms as the most strongly CT-179-down-regulated transcripts at the early time point and showed correlated β-tubulin and OLIG2 expression in TCGA glioblastoma specimens. Combination with the Mcl-1 inhibitor S63845 or the Bcl-2/Bcl-xL/Bcl-w inhibitor ABT-737 produced greater-than-additive cytotoxicity. Oral CT-179 crossed the blood-brain barrier and extended median survival as a single agent across two independent adult orthotopic patient-derived backgrounds (GBM8 and G06); intraperitoneal CT-179 was associated with reduced intratumoral OLIG2 and Ki-67 staining in GBM8 orthotopic xenografts. Combination of CT-179 with radiotherapy and temozolomide eliminated all GBM8 and 7 of 8 GBM4 subcutaneous xenografts without weight loss and significantly extended survival when combined with radiotherapy in MGMT-unmethylated GBM6 orthotopic xenografts (CT-179 administered intraperitoneally). Conclusions CT-179 is a brain-penetrant inhibitor of an established GBM driver with single-agent and combination activity across several orthotopic models, supporting clinical development for GBM and translational evaluation in other OLIG2-dependent CNS malignancies. Key Points CT-179 is the first brain-penetrant small-molecule inhibitor of OLIG2 with potent activity across patient-derived glioblastoma models. CT-179 induces apoptosis through mitotic catastrophe and slippage rather than collapse of receptor tyrosine kinase signaling. Oral CT-179 combined with radiotherapy and temozolomide eliminates the great majority of subcutaneous patient-derived GBM xenografts without overt toxicity. Oral CT-179 extends single-agent survival across two independent adult orthotopic patient-derived backgrounds (GBM8 and G06); intraperitoneal CT-179 is associated with reduced intratumoral OLIG2 and Ki-67 staining in GBM8 tumors. Intraperitoneal CT-179 plus radiotherapy significantly extends survival in an MGMT-unmethylated GBM6 orthotopic model where temozolomide contributes minimally and supports the rationale for further evaluation in MGMT-unmethylated GBM. Importance of the Study Glioblastoma is uniformly fatal, and durable disease-modifying therapies that disable the lineage transcription factor programs sustaining the GBM stem-like state have remained elusive. OLIG2 is universally expressed in diffuse glioma and is a central driver of stemness, lineage-restricted RTK signaling, and resistance to genotoxic therapy, yet has historically been considered undruggable. This study reports the foundational preclinical characterization of CT-179, a brain-penetrant small molecule that engages OLIG2 directly and induces glioblastoma cell death through disrupted mitotic progression. Oral CT-179 crosses the blood-brain barrier, prolongs survival in orthotopic patient-derived xenografts, and substantially enhances the efficacy of standard-of-care radiotherapy and temozolomide. Activity in an MGMT-unmethylated orthotopic patient-derived GBM model in combination with radiotherapy is of particular translational interest, since this is the patient population for which temozolomide contributes minimally and the unmet need is greatest. These data establish proof of concept for direct pharmacologic inhibition of OLIG2 in GBM and provide a translational rationale, including an MGMT-stratified combination strategy, for combining CT-179 with current standard-of-care chemoradiotherapy. Lay Summary Glioblastoma is the most common and aggressive brain cancer in adults, and almost all patients die of their disease. One reason is a protein called OLIG2, which keeps tumor cells in an immature, treatment-resistant state and has long been considered impossible to target with drugs. We studied CT-179, a small molecule that enters the brain and blocks OLIG2. In glioblastoma cells and in mice, CT-179 forced dividing tumor cells into a faulty, lethal division, extended survival on its own, and strengthened the effect of standard radiation and chemotherapy. These results support testing CT-179 in people with glioblastoma.

title: Longitudinal associations between neuropsychiatric symptoms, structural and perfusion MRI changes in older adults with Mild Cognitive Impairment
abstract: Neuropsychiatric symptoms (NPS) are highly prevalent in Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI), conceptualized as an intermediate clinical state between normal aging and dementia. Although neuroimaging studies have reported associations between NPS and brain alterations in MCI, longitudinal evidence on NPS and their relationship with multimodal MRI measures remains limited. We aimed to investigate (1) longitudinal changes in NPS, volumetric assessment and measurement of regional cerebral blood flow (CBF) within the medial temporal lobe (MTL); (2) associations between longitudinal changes in MRI measures and NPS; (3) whether baseline MRI measures predicted longitudinal changes in NPS. Thirty individuals with MCI aged over 65 years were recruited, of whom eighteen followed up for a mean period of 29 ± 8.9 months. There were significant reductions in total grey matter and white matter volumes, together with volume loss in the bilateral hippocampus, bilateral parahippocampal gyrus and right entorhinal cortex (p FDR< 0.05) over the follow up period. Volume loss in the right parahippocampal gyrus was associated with increase in aggression (p FDR <0.01), and CBF increase in the right hippocampus and parahippocampal gyrus was associated with worsening in agitation (p FDR <0.01). Furthermore, lower baseline volume of the right entorhinal cortex was associated with increase in aggression, and lower baseline CBF in the right hippocampus and parahippocampal gyrus was associated with worsening of agitation (p FDR <0.05). Our findings highlight the importance of identifying NPS in individuals with MCI and the role of structural and perfusion MRI measures as promising biomarkers for monitoring disease progression and improving risk prediction of conversion to dementia.

title: Vascular Proximity Coverage: A Novel CT-Based Marker of Pulmonary Vascular Distance to the Lung Parenchyma
abstract: RationaleConventional CT-derived pulmonary vascular metrics quantify vascular pruning but do not assess spatial heterogeneity of vascular architecture. In COPD, peripheral microvascular pruning coexists with compensatory central vessel dilation, paradoxically preserving total vessel volume while reducing effective vascular penetration into lung parenchyma. ObjectivesTo develop and validate Vascular Proximity Coverage (VPC), a novel distance-based CT biomarker quantifying spatial efficiency of pulmonary vascular distribution. MethodsThis retrospective analysis included 7,881 COPDGene participants with complete vascular segmentations. VPC is estimated by integrating the area under the cumulative lung tissue coverage curve at distances 0-10 mm from segmented vessel voxels. Multivariable models were used to assess associations with lung function, six-minute walk distance (6MWD), St. Georges Respiratory Questionnaire (SGRQ), mMRC dyspnea score and all-cause mortality adjusting for demographics, smoking, emphysema, scanner type, and BV5. We stratified the cohort into four groups defined by the median values of BV5 and VPC, yielding discordant (high-BV5/low-VPC, low-BV5/high-VPC) and concordant (high/high, low/low) vascular phenotypes. ResultsVPC declined across disease severity (5.82 {+/-} 0.50 in non-smokers to 5.21 {+/-} 0.64 in GOLD 4; p<0.001). Among spirometrically normal smokers, current smokers showed reduced VPC versus former smokers (5.31 vs. 5.68; p<0.001). Each standard deviation (SD) decrease in VPC was independently associated with reduced 6MWD ({beta}=-16.8 m, 95% CI: -19.5 to -14.0), worse SGRQ ({beta}=1.9, 95% CI: 1.4 to 2.4), and increased dyspnea (RR=1.05, 95% CI: 1.03-1.08; all p<0.001). The lowest VPC quartile, as compared to the reference quartile, was associated with 38% higher mortality (HR=1.38, 95% CI: 1.18-1.62; p<0.001). Based on median thresholds, high-BV5/low-VPC phenotype, compared to High-BV5/High-VPC, showed 24% increased mortality (HR=1.24, 95% CI: 1.08-1.42; p=0.002) despite preserved vessel volume. ConclusionsVPC captures spatial heterogeneity of vascular architecture independent of vessel volume and detects subclinical vascular dysfunction in smokers without airflow obstruction. AT A GLANCE COMMENTARYO_ST_ABSScientific Knowledge on the SubjectC_ST_ABSCurrent CT-based pulmonary vascular metrics, including volume of blood vessels less than 5 mm{superscript 2} cross-sectional area (BV5) and total vessel volume, quantify the amount of visible vasculature but do not assess how effectively vessels reach the lung parenchyma for efficient gas exchange. In COPD, peripheral microvascular pruning commonly coexists with compensatory central vessel dilation, leading to preserved or increased total vascular volume despite compromised functional vascular distribution. What This Study Adds to the FieldVascular Proximity Coverage (VPC) is a novel distance-based CT biomarker that quantifies the spatial efficiency of pulmonary vascular distribution by measuring cumulative lung tissue coverage across distances from vessel walls. In 7,881 COPDGene participants, including non-smokers and PRISm subjects, lower VPC was independently associated with decreased lung function, reduced exercise capacity, worsened quality of life, and increased all-cause mortality over a median 10.8-year follow-up after adjusting for BV5 and emphysema. VPC identified a high-risk phenotype with preserved vessel volume but impaired distribution (high-BV5/low-VPC) that carried 24% increased mortality risk and detected subclinical vascular dysfunction in smokers with normal spirometry.

title: Interictal functional ultrasound imaging in human epilepsy resection and responsive neurostimulation surgery
abstract: Over 30% of patients with epilepsy are refractory to medication and may require surgical or neuromodulation-based intervention. Accurate localization of seizure-onset zones (SOZ) and assessment of treatment-associated brain responses remain major clinical challenges. Current workflows may involve invasive intracranial monitoring, prolonged hospitalization, adjustment of anti-seizure medications, and seizure capture to localize the SOZ, while opportunities for complementary intraoperative functional assessment remain limited. We used intraoperative functional ultrasound imaging (fUSI) to characterize interictal (i.e., non-seizure) cortical activity in nine patients with drug-resistant focal epilepsy and to assess treatment-associated brain responses following SOZ resection and responsive neurostimulation (RNS). fUSI signals were acquired directly from the exposed cortex during standard-of-care surgery. We developed six ultrafast power Doppler-based interictal activity markers (IaMs) to distinguish SOZ from peri-resection zone (PRZ) cortex and to quantify treatment-associated changes. The IaMs revealed distinct interictal hemodynamic dynamics between SOZ and PRZ cortex. Following SOZ resection, all six markers changed significantly within the surrounding PRZ. RNS also induced robust, stimulation paradigm-dependent modulation of cortical hemodynamic dynamics. Notably, RNS and surgical resection produced concordant directional changes across five of the six IaMs, despite representing fundamentally different therapeutic interventions. Together, these findings demonstrate the feasibility of intraoperative fUSI for characterizing and distinguishing interictal dynamics within SOZ and PRZ cortex and assessing treatment-associated cortical responses during human epilepsy surgery. Furthermore, fUSI could provide a complementary high-resolution functional imaging approach alongside established clinical methods for SOZ localization and intraoperative functional assessment.

title: Distinct spatial organization of human hippocampal perfusion and microvascular pulsatility across age
abstract: Arterial pulsation can modulate neuronal activity through mechanosensitive pathways in mice, but whether vascular pulsatility is similarly related to neural organization in humans remains unclear. Here, using 7T MRI in 35 young and older adults, we mapped cerebral perfusion and microvascular volumetric pulsatility index (mvPI) across the unfolded hippocampus and integrated these measures with histological, electrophysiological, and transcriptomic reference maps. Perfusion and mvPI exhibited distinct spatial organization and age-related differences. In young adults, perfusion preferentially corresponded to parvalbumin-interneuron density and beta/gamma distribution, whereas mvPI was associated with theta-band distribution. A number of associations detected in young adults were not detected in the older adults maps. Spectral simulations showed qualitative similarity to heartbeat-related phase resetting as one possible explanation for the mvPI–theta relationship, while spatial transcriptomics revealed perivascular enrichment of PIEZO2 , a candidate mediator of vascular mechanotransduction. Together, these findings establish perfusion and tissue-level pulsatility as distinct dimensions of human hippocampal vascular organization and provide a framework for investigating their relationships with neural dynamics across aging.

title: Understanding Performance Plateaus and Representation Collapse in 3D MRI Transformers Trained to Classify Brain Disease
abstract: In medical imaging AI, we commonly assume that diagnostic classifiers will increase in accuracy if they are trained on more data, but in reality, their performance often plateaus. To understand this behavior, we ran a spectral analysis of 3D vision transformers, a common supervised deep learning model that can be trained to classify disease based on 3D brain MRI. For simpler classification methods such as linear discriminant analysis, the classifier performance AUC(N), when trained on a sample of size N, is known to depend on the encoder′s eigenspectrum. Each class-discriminative direction in the latent space contributes only after the sample size N reaches a threshold, so the spectrum influences how performance scales with training data. Building on this theory, we show that supervised transformers compress almost all of their discriminative signal into one principal component (EVR@1 = 0.90—0.96): after this representation collapse happens, no further directions cross the threshold as training data increases, and accuracy plateaus. In principle, this plateau in performance could be due to either the encoder′s learned feature space or the difficulty of the task. To distinguish these cases, we trained three types of supervised 3D transformers (ViT3D, MINiT, NIT) and, as a non-collapsing alternative, a frozen self-supervised encoder (DINO), to classify people with dementia or mild cognitive impairment (MCI) versus cognitively normal (CN) individuals from 3D brain MRI, using data from the Alzheimer′s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI). We froze each encoder and applied it to a new task, so that only the task difficulty varied. An easy task encoder (Dementia vs CN), transferred to the harder task (MCI vs CN), did not reproduce the plateau (MINiT threshold 9.2), but full retraining did (2758.5). The plateau is therefore due to the learned encoder, rather than task difficulty. Ranking the feature directions by the proportion of the disease signal they contain, we were able to identify a sign of representation collapse, i.e., a single dominant spike in the latent feature eigenspectrum. This spike was 11—26 times larger than predicted from the rest of the spectrum for the disease-trained (supervised) encoders, but was absent for DINO (0.66). To predict how transformer accuracy scales with the number of training scans, a large spike in the encoder spectrum suggests that the representation has collapsed and additional scans will not help; a small spike means that the signal is spread across many encoder latent space directions, and more training data should boost the classifier performance.

title: Beyond Agrammatism: Syntax Processing in Chinese Primary Progressive Aphasia
abstract: Syntax processing impairment is a defining feature of primary progressive aphasia (PPA), particularly in the nonfluent/agrammatic variant. However, current models are derived largely from Indo-European languages, and it remains unclear whether the cognitive and neuroanatomical mechanisms of syntax processing generalize to Chinese, an analytic, pro-drop language that encodes grammatical relationships primarily through word order and function words rather than inflectional morphology. Participants were recruited from the international Chinese Language Assessment in PPA cohort and included 64 individuals with PPA (19 logopenic, 15 nonfluent/agrammatic, 15 semantic, and 15 unclassifiable/mixed) and 60 cognitively healthy controls. Participants completed sentence comprehension and production tasks with systematically manipulated syntactic features. Item-level linguistic determinants were examined using ridge regression, diagnostic performance using receiver operating characteristic analyses, and neuroanatomical correlates using voxel-based morphometry of structural MRI. Performance on sentence comprehension and production was influenced by grammatical and lexical features. Subject-relative clauses, passive constructions, a higher proportion of function words, longer character length, and greater lexical content were associated with poorer performance among participants with PPA. Sentence comprehension was impaired in the logopenic, nonfluent/agrammatic, and semantic variants, even when isolated to the syntactic component of the sentence comprehension task. Similarly, sentence production was impaired across all PPA variants (all P < 0.01 versus controls). No significant differences were observed among PPA variants. Adjusted receiver operating characteristic analyses demonstrated high discrimination between each PPA variant and controls, with areas under the curve ranging from 0.87 to 0.97 for sentence comprehension-syntax and from 0.91 to 0.97 for sentence production. However, pairwise comparisons showed no significant differences in discriminative performance among PPA variants after correction for multiple comparisons. Both sentence comprehension-syntax and sentence production showed associations with semantic and repetition measures in addition to motor speech measures. Voxel-based morphometry showed that higher sentence comprehension-syntax scores were associated with greater grey matter volume in left frontotemporal and cingulate regions, whereas higher sentence production scores were additionally associated with greater gray matter volume in frontostriatal structures, including the caudate, putamen, and thalamus. Syntactic processing impairment in Chinese-speaking individuals with PPA extends beyond the nonfluent/agrammatic variant and is associated with distributed frontotemporal and frontostriatal regions, as well as lexical-semantic and auditory verbal short term memory mechanisms. These findings suggest that the cognitive and neural manifestations of syntactic impairment may be shaped by language-specific typological properties, underscoring the need for linguistically informed approaches to the assessment and interpretation of PPA.

title: Clinicopathologic Predictors of PSMA-PET Detection, Recurrence Pattern, and Biochemical Outcome Following Salvage Radiotherapy After Radical Prostatectomy
abstract: Purpose Biochemical recurrence (BCR) after radical prostatectomy (RP) presents heterogeneous recurrence patterns and variable outcomes following salvage radiotherapy (sRT). We evaluated clinicopathologic determinants of PSMA-PET/CT detection, anatomical recurrence distribution, and biochemical disease-free survival (bDFS) following PSMA-PET-guided sRT. Methods This retrospective single-institution study included 140 patients with BCR after RP who underwent 68 Ga-PSMA-PET/CT prior to sRT with or without androgen deprivation therapy. PSMA-PET-positive findings were categorized as prostate bed only (PBO) or pelvic nodal involvement with or without the prostate bed (PLNI). Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, logistic regression, and Cox proportional hazards models were employed. Results PSMA-PET detected locoregional recurrence in 77/140 patients (55%). On multivariable analysis, PSA at recurrence (OR=2.07; p=0.003) and age (OR=1.07; p=0.016) were the sole independent predictors of PSMA-PET positivity. ROC analysis yielded AUC=0.74 (optimal threshold of 0.58 ng/mL). Among PSMA-positive patients, PBO was associated with a longer time to BCR (tBCR) (37.5 versus 15 months; p=0.006). Seminal vesicle invasion (SVI) and pT-stage predicted PLNI on univariable analysis. Among 124 of 140 evaluable patients (median follow-up 31 months), estimated bDFS at 24, 36, and 60 months was 89.7%, 80.2%, and 54.1%, respectively. SVI (HR=2.39; p=0.031), EPE (HR=2.82; p=0.012), pT-stage (HR=1.64; p=0.021), and pN-stage (HR=1.83; p=0.045) were associated with increased failure on univariable Cox regression, though none retained independent significance. Conclusion PSA burden and age independently predicted PSMA-PET detection. Recurrence patterns reflected disease behavior, as PBO was associated with longer tBCR. Adverse pathologic features were associated with pelvic nodal disease and reduced biochemical control; none remained independently predictive.

Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, logistic regression, and Cox proportional hazards models were employed.

Results

PSMA-PET detected locoregional recurrence in 77/140 patients (55%). On multivariable analysis, PSA at recurrence (OR=2.07; p=0.003) and age (OR=1.07; p=0.016) were the sole independent predictors of PSMA-PET positivity. title: Deep Learning-Based Anatomical Level Classification of Craniofacial CT Slices: Comparison of CNN Architectures and Ensemble Methods
abstract: Computed tomography (CT) interpretation requires recognition of the anatomical level of each slice. Classification may facilitate preprocessing and AI-assisted fracture diagnosis. We developed deep learning models to classify craniofacial CT slices into six anatomical categories. A total of 11,769 images were collected from a multicenter database involving 10 Japanese university hospitals and the public Head-Neck-Radiomics-HN1 dataset. Patients were divided into training (70%) and evaluation (30%) sets. Five CNN architectures were trained from scratch, and hard- and soft-voting ensembles were evaluated. Individual-model accuracy ranged from 94.72% to 96.09%; the hard-voting ensemble achieved 96.46% accuracy (Cohens {kappa} = 0.954). Although performance differed among individual models (Cochrans Q = 99.29, p < 0.001), the ensemble did not significantly outperform EfficientNetV2B1 (McNemars p = 0.163). Errors occurred mainly between adjacent anatomical regions. Deep learning can classify craniofacial CT slices accurately and may support automated dataset organization and AI-assisted fracture diagnosis. External validation is needed.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Fine Needle Aspiration Cytology in Thyroid Diseases: Comparison with Histopathological Findings in Hawassa, Ethiopia
abstract: Introduction Thyroid diseases are major health problems and among the most common endocrine disorders worldwide, including in Ethiopia. They are characterized by alterations in hormone secretion, enlargement of the thyroid gland, or both. Fine needle aspiration cytology is an important initial screening tool, and histopathologic examination is essential for the definitive diagnosis of thyroid disease. This study aimed to compare the diagnostic accuracy of fine needle aspiration cytology with histopathology in identifying thyroid diseases. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted at three health facilities in Hawassa City, Ethiopia, involving 304 patients who underwent both thyroid fine needle aspiration cytology and histopathologic examination of the same site between 30 th October 2024 and 29 th October 2025. FNAC results were classified using the Bethesda system, with histopathology as the gold standard. Data were entered into Kobo Toolbox, exported to SPSS version 27, and analyzed using cross-tabulation and chi-square (χ 2 ) tests to determine diagnostic accuracy. Result 304 patient records were included in the study. The fine needle aspiration cytology was determinate/diagnostic in 81.6% of cases. The study revealed the sensitivity and specificity of fine needle aspiration cytology to be 88.2% (CI 77.6-95.1%) and 94.4% (CI 90.6-97.1%), respectively. The false negative and false positive rates in this study were 2.4% and 4.4%, respectively. The positive predictive value was 80.3% (CI 68.7-89.3%), and the negative predictive value was 96.8% (CI 93.8-98.7%). The accuracy of fine needle aspiration cytology in differentiating benign from malignant thyroid lesions was 93.1%. Conclusion FNAC demonstrated strong agreement with histopathology and remains a reliable, cost-effective first-line diagnostic tool for thyroid disease, particularly in resource-limited settings. Strengthening sample handling, ultrasound guidance, and adherence to Bethesda criteria may further improve diagnostic precision

title: Neurochemical fingerprinting of the Alzheimers disease continuum using 7 T short-echo-time brain single voxel 1H-MRS.
abstract: IntroductionThis study aimed to characterize the neurochemical profile of Alzheimers disease (AD) continuum stages using proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy (1H-MRS) data for brain metabolites and macromolecules. We used Orthogonal Projection to Latent Structures Discriminant Analysis (OPLS-DA) to classify diagnostic groups and assess feature importance. MethodsOur dataset consisted of 7 T short-echo time 1H-MRS spectra of the posterior cingulate cortex/precuneus of individuals diagnosed with AD (n = 27) or Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI, n = 27) and Healthy Controls (HC, n = 31). Classification used 100-round Monte Carlo cross-validation based on metabolite concentrations and macromolecular peak intensities. Variable importance in projection (VIP) was assessed across classification models to identify the most relevant neurochemical features. The resulting metabolite rankings were compared with previous literature to evaluate their biological plausibility. ResultsClassification was strongest for AD versus HC (AUC=0.88) and lower for comparisons involving MCI. Metabolites contributing most strongly to classification included myo-inositol, ascorbate, and choline-containing compounds, consistent with previous studies on AD-related neurochemical alterations. In addition, specific macromolecular components were identified as relevant features, suggesting a potential contribution of MM signals to the characterization of AD-related neurochemistry. DiscussionThese findings support the use of short-echo-time 1H-MRS as a complementary tool for characterizing neurochemical changes in the AD continuum, with potential applications in disease characterization and monitoring, warranting validation in larger cohorts.

title: Preclinical Evaluation of [ 18 F]Itareparib, a brain penetrant PARP1-selective radioligand, in Glioma Rat Model and Nonhuman Primate
abstract: ABSTRACT Rationale Poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase-1 (PARP1) is a central mediator of DNA damage response and is upregulated in glioma, supporting it as a molecular imaging biomarker. However, quantitative PET assessment of PARP1 in infiltrative tumors with a preserved blood-brain barrier remains an unmet need. In this study, we evaluated if [ 18 F]Itareparib, a brain-penetrant, non-trapping, PARP1-selective radioligand with reversible kinetics, could improve brain tumor diagnosis and enable target occupancy studies in neurooncology. Methods [ 18 F]Itareparib was synthesized and evaluated in an orthotopic rat model of BT142 IDH1-mutant gliomas. Dynamic PET scans were performed with or without the administration of the PARP1-selective inhibitor AZD9574. Standardized uptake value ratios (SUVRs) for tumors were calculated using the contralateral region as reference and compared with distribution volume ratios (DVRs) calculated using kinetic modeling. PARP1-specific binding and tracer stability were assessed using autoradiography, immunofluorescence, biodistribution, and radiometabolite analysis. Brain kinetics of [ 18 F]Itareparib were evaluated in a healthy nonhuman primate (NHP) at baseline and blocking conditions. Results [ 18 F]Itareparib rapidly entered the rat brains and showed 4-fold higher uptake in BT142 tumors than in the contralateral brain. AZD9574 reduced tumor uptake by 77%, supporting the PARP1-specific binding of [ 18 F]Itareparib in the tumors. SUVR (30–60 min) showed the closest agreement with DVR. Autoradiographic tumor-to-reference mean ratio was 7.3, and AZD9574 reduced the tumor-to-reference ratio by 56%. PARP1 immunofluorescence was higher in tumor than the rest of the brain and correlated with autoradiographic results. In rats, the parent fraction of [ 18 F]Itareparib exceeded 99% in brain through 60 min post tracer injection ( p.i. ) and was approximately 88% in plasma at 60 min p.i. In the NHP, [ 18 F]Itareparib showed rapid brain uptake, and V T decreased by 21 ± 6 % after blocking with AZD9574. Conclusion [ 18 F]Itareparib showed brain penetration, high in vivo metabolic stability, reversible binding kinetics, and PARP1-specific tumor uptake. These findings support further development of [ 18 F]Itareparib for the quantitative PET imaging of PARP1 in brain tumors.

title: Aberrant cortical reorganization and astrogliosis underlie memory deficit post-traumatic brain injury: a longitudinal multiscale multimodal study
abstract: THE BIGGER PICTURE We now have imaging and analytical tools to study the brain at multiple scales, from scanning the whole brain to see how different neuronal networks interact to scrutinizing individual cells. However, multimodal and multiscale investigations are challenging to conduct in the same subject and generate copious amounts of complex data. Such experimental designs are invaluable in studying heterogeneous neurological disease with pathology at both cellular and network level. Using traumatic brain injury as a test case, we conducted macroscale MRI imaging as well as 3D whole-brain light-sheet fluorescence microscopy with cellular resolution to study network dysfunction and markers of cognitive deficits post-injury. We identified sensitive neurophysiological markers that distinguish healthy and injured mice, and predicted their memory capabilities. The framework we present is broadly applicable to understanding complex cognitive functions and identifying the physiological correlates of distributed network dysfunction in neurological disorders. HIGHLIGHTS ● Multiscale framework integration of in vivo MRI and ex vivo whole-brain histology ● Connectomic gradients reveal network dedifferentiation linked to memory deficit ● 3D whole-brain segmentation show neuronal hyperactivity and widespread astrogliosis ● AI-based axon tracing reveals persistent damage despite normal neuroimaging scans SUMMARY Integrating high-dimensional neuroimaging data across spatial scales remains a fundamental bottleneck in quantitative neuroscience. Here, we apply emerging analytical techniques including functional connectome gradient mapping and 3D segmentation of whole-brain cellular resolution microscopy data in a mouse model of traumatic brain injury. At the macroscale, longitudinal functional MRI revealed a transition from frontal hyperconnectivity to hippocampal hypoconnectivity and unimodal-transmodal gradient contraction indicating network dedifferentiation. At the cellular scale, deep-learning based segmentation of whole-brain light-sheet fluorescence microscopy volumes quantified regional astrogliosis, neuronal hyperactivity, and single-axon loss undetected by standard diffusion MRI. Multiscale multimodal data integration not only identified quantitative biomarkers predictive of memory performance post-injury but also enabled validation of in vivo modalities against more sensitive ex vivo histology. This study demonstrates a framework for probing complex multi-network cognitive functions and neurological disorders of network dysfunction.

title: TiSAM: fusing spatial and histopathology foundation models for whole-slide image segmentation
abstract: Semantic segmentation of whole-slide images (WSIs) quantifies tissue composition and architecture, but existing models require extensive annotation and lose accuracy as the number of tissue classes increases or on heterogeneous, cross-scanner datasets. Here, we present the Tissue Segment Anything Model (TiSAM), which fuses SAM3 spatial features with UNI2-h pathology features within a multi-scale decoder. Because public benchmarks contain few tissue classes, we release MegaMouse, comprising 36,833 annotations of 52 tissue classes from 12 mouse organs, and an 11-class human pancreas dataset. TiSAM achieved the highest overall performance across four public datasets compared to existing convolutional neural network and vision transformer models, maintained high accuracy on MegaMouse, and maintained high accuracy in the human pancreas dataset when trained on as few as 5 annotated WSIs where previous integrations of SAM with pathology foundation models did not. TiSAM segmentations were also more consistent across eight slide scanners compared to other models. These results establish TiSAM as a general and highly adaptable framework for tissue segmentation, enabling studies containing many tissue classes, limited annotations, or images from multiple scanners.

title: Claims-based reconstruction of the pancreatic cancer care pathway links centralization of care to survival
abstract: Background The organization of pancreatic cancer care may be associated with survival. Using health administrative claims data, we reconstructed the pathway from diagnosis to first-line therapy and examined associations of multidisciplinary team review and treatment at specialized centers with overall survival. Methods Longitudinal historical cohort study using anonymized health administrative claims data from six Czech health insurance funds, covering approximately 17% of patients diagnosed with pancreatic cancer nationally between 2018 and 2020. Adults with an incident ICD-10 C25 record confirmed by imaging and histopathology were followed from the index date (the date of the first qualifying imaging or histopathological examination) until death, censoring, or 31 December 2021. Overall survival was analyzed using Kaplan–Meier methods and Cox regression adjusted for age and first-line therapy type. Results Of 1,255 patients, 920 (73.3%) received first-line therapy and 266 (21.2%) died untreated. Among treated patients, 436 (47.4%) underwent multidisciplinary team review, 335 (36.4%) underwent surgery, and 667 (72.5%) were treated at a complex oncological center. Surgery was associated with longer overall survival than chemotherapy (age-adjusted hazard ratio [HR] 0.32, P < 0.001). Treatment at a complex oncological center was associated with longer overall survival (adjusted HR 0.77, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.64–0.92, P = 0.004; crude median 532 versus 394 days). Multidisciplinary team review was not significantly associated with overall survival (adjusted HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.73–1.01, P = 0.073). Conclusions Treatment at a complex oncological center was associated with longer survival, while fewer than half of patients had a recorded multidisciplinary team review. How care is organized, not only which therapy is delivered, is associated with outcome. The observational design and absence of key clinical covariates limit causal interpretation.

title: Morphometric Brain Networks at Ultra-Low Field: A First Assessment of Feasibility and Reliability
abstract: BackgroundUltra-low field (ULF) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) offers accessible point-of-care neuroimag-ing, yet its capability to support multivariate network analyses remains understudied. MethodsWe systematically evaluated the feasibility and reliability of Morphometric Similarity Networks (MSN) and Morphometric Inverse Divergence (MIND) networks derived from paired high-field (HF, 3T/1.5T) and ULF (64mT) scans in a primary cohort (N=23) and an independent replication cohort (N=19). We tested the impact of super-resolution processing, cortical parcellation granularity (Desikan-Killiany vs. Destrieux), and mesh resolution (fsnative vs. fsaverage5) on edge-level cross-scanner agreement (Lins concordance correlation coefficient, CCC) and subject-level identifiability. ResultsMIND networks demonstrated higher edge-level HF-ULF agreement (mean CCC = 0.95) and ULF reproducibility (mean CCC = 0.98) compared to MSNs (mean CCC = 0.86-0.87 and 0.91-0.94, respectively). In contrast, MSNs yielded higher subject-level differential identifiability across field strengths due to a broader dis-tinction between within- and between-subject similarity. Reconstructing MIND networks on native high-resolution meshes (fsnative) maximised cross-scanner agreement, whereas coarser meshes and finer cortical parcellations enhanced individual network identifiability. ConclusionsStructural similarity networks can be reliably constructed from ULF MRI data. Optimal analytic choices depend on study objectives: MIND on native meshes maximises cross-scanner stability, whereas MSNs excel at preserving individual uniqueness, paving the way for globally scalable connectomic research.

title: Clinical referral text overrides MRI evidence in multimodal large language models: glioma versus brain abscess
abstract: ObjectivesTo determine how strongly clinical referral text, rather than image content, drives the decisions of multimodal large language models (LLMs) differentiating glioma from brain abscess on MRI. Materials and methodsThis retrospective single-center study included 60 contrast-enhanced T1-weighted brain MRI examinations (30 gliomas, 30 abscesses; reference-standard diagnosis). One axial slice per case was paired with five referral texts (explicitly inflammatory to explicitly tumor-suggestive) under three prompt instructions and submitted 20 times each to GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 5, Gemini 3.5 Flash, and Qwen 3.6 (72,000 answers). The primary outcome was the text-driven span (difference in tumor-call frequency between explicit inflammatory and explicit tumor text). Two blinded radiologists classified the images without text; sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy were compared descriptively. ResultsPatients (29 women) had a mean age of 55.8 {+/-} 16.4 years. With neutral text, models answered tumor in 45-67% of queries (specificity, 0.38-0.78), versus 52% and 60% for radiologists (specificity, 0.77 and 0.63). The text-driven span was 0.79-1.00 (p < 0.001 for all models), whereas confirmed gliomas and abscesses differed by only 0.01-0.10 in three models and 0.25 in Gemini 3.5 Flash. Subtle wording produced at least 83% of the span in three models. An instruction to ignore the text reduced the span to 0.48-0.70 in three models and to 0.04 in Gemini 3.5 Flash, partly through reversion to a tumor default. Model accuracy was 0.52-0.73 versus 0.78 and 0.73 for radiologists. ConclusionMultimodal LLMs deferred to referral text over imaging evidence in differentiating glioma from brain abscess, and prompt instructions did not reliably correct this. Key PointsO_ST_ABSQuestionC_ST_ABSMultimodal large language models receive images together with clinical referral text, but how strongly the text rather than the image determines their diagnosis is unknown. FindingsChanging only the referral text largely reversed the glioma-versus-abscess decision for identical MRI images in four models; instructions to ignore the text reduced this inconsistently. Clinical relevanceBefore clinical use, multimodal large language models require model- and task-specific testing of their susceptibility to referral text, because instructing them to prioritize the image is not a dependable safeguard against text-driven misdiagnosis.

title: Beyond Segmentation Accuracy: Evaluating Biological Fidelity in Spatial Pathology
abstract: Multiplex immunofluorescence (MxIF) resolves cellular identity, state, and spatial organization within tumor tissue, enabling higher-order representations of cancer ecosystems including immune infiltration, multicellular neighborhoods, and tissue niches. Yet these analyses depend on a deceptively simple first step: accurately identifying individual cells. Segmentation errors can alter marker quantification, cellular phenotypes, cell–cell relationships, and ultimately the spatial organization inferred from an image. Consequently, improvements in conventional segmentation benchmarks matter biologically only if they propagate to more faithful representations of the tumor microenvironment. We test this relationship directly using an expert-curated benchmark of 31,924 expert-reviewed cells on three slides under a leave-slide-out protocol. We compare a domain-specific self-supervised encoder, adapted to multiplex tissue imaging, with supervised, microscopy-specific, prompted generalist, and general-purpose vision models, and pass every method’s predicted cells through an identical downstream pipeline. We evaluate fidelity across four levels: cell segmentation, phenotype assignment, spatial neighborhood structure, and tissue organization, comprising niches and tumor–immune interactions. The resulting hierarchy reveals that these levels do not improve in lockstep. Cellular phenotype assignment is comparatively robust to segmentation differences, whereas missed cells increasingly disrupt neighborhood structure and tumor–immune interactions. As a stringent spatial-interaction test, tumor–CD8 + contact recovery is poorly predicted by conventional segmentation quality (Panoptic Quality: ρ = 0.18), while errors specifically at tumor–immune interfaces are strongly associated with contact fidelity ( ρ = −0.80). Methods with nearly identical segmentation accuracy can therefore produce substantially different biological representations. These results argue that cell segmentation for spatial pathology should be evaluated not only by boundary and instance accuracy, but also by preservation of the biological relationships that downstream analyses are intended to measure.

title: Scaled m-BonacciNet: A Recurrence-Guided Lightweight CNN for Efficient Medical Image Classification
abstract: The m-Bonacci weighted sequence space [Formula] is introduced for m [≥]2, 1[≤]p < {infty}, and > 0. It is proved to be a Banach space isometrically isomorphic to lp, with an unconditional Schauder basis. The space is also reflexive and uniformly convex. Its strict inclusion chain, continuous dual, and asymptotic truncation estimate of order[Formula] are established. Based on this framework, Scaled m-BonacciNet is proposed as a lightweight CNN that rescales Fibonacci-Net channels using the dominant m-Bonacci root and employs depthwise separable convolutions. Tribonacci-Net achieved 96.09% accuracy and 0.9581 macro F1-score on the 15-class Brain MRI dataset using 0.85 million parameters and 0.366 GFLOPs. Pentanacci-Net attained 95.87% accuracy on the 44-class dataset, reducing parameters and FLOPs by 47.10% and 44.48%. Hexanacci-Net achieved 83.75% accuracy and 0.7941 macro F1-score on CKD ultrasound.

title: Individual-level Structural Neuroimaging Biomarkers across the Psychosis Spectrum
abstract: ABSTRACT Background and Hypothesis Although psychotic disorders are characterized by widespread cortical thinning, translating these findings into individualized biomarkers remains challenging. Regional Vulnerability Index (RVI) and Neuroscore are candidate individual-level biomarkers that quantify the similarity between an individual’s structural brain pattern and generic psychosis-associated alterations. This study investigated cortical thickness (CT)-based RVI and Neuroscore, along with mean CT deviation from healthy individuals, across the psychosis spectrum. Study Design Using structural 3T MRI data from 289 participants (clinical high risk for psychosis [CHR], n=39; first episode psychosis [FEP], n=44, chronic psychosis [CP], n=86; healthy controls [HC], n=120), RVI, Neuroscore, and mean CT deviation (z) scores were computed from region-wise CT measures quantified using FreeSurfer v7.2. Group differences and associations with symptoms were evaluated. Study Results RVI and Neuroscore were significantly higher, and mean CT z-scores lower, in FEP and CP compared with CHR and HC, with moderate-to-large effect sizes (|Cohen’s d| = 0.55–1.15). No differences were observed between FEP and CP or CHR and HC. Indices were not associated with psychosis-spectrum symptom severity in the CHR, FEP, or CP groups. RVI ( r = −0.561, p < .001) and Neuroscore ( r = −0.997, p < .001) were strongly negatively correlated with the mean CT z-score. Conclusions CT-based RVI and Neuroscore appear to index established disease status but not risk status, while showing substantial overlap with mean CT deviation. These findings highlight the need to further refine these biomarkers through data-driven and multimodal approaches to improve their utility for risk and prognostic prediction.

title: Anatomically Programmable and Optically Tunable 3D-Bioprinted Tumor-Mimicking Phantoms for Quantitative Nanofluorophore Benchmarking
abstract: Surgical resection remains a primary treatment for solid tumors, with fluorescence-guided surgery offering improved intraoperative visualization and precision. However, conventional murine models provide limited control over anatomical and optical variables critical to evaluating fluorescent imaging agents. Here, we developed 3D-bioprinted, anatomically tailored and optically tunable tumor-mimicking phantoms (TMPs) as a reproducible platform for quantitative nanofluorophore evaluation under tissue-relevant surgical conditions. These TMPs recreate subcutaneous, epithelial, and intraperitoneal tumor presentations while enabling controlled variation of lesion geometry, spatial distribution, tissue pigmentation, cellular composition, and nanofluorophore concentration. Semiconducting polymer nanofluorophores (SPNs) with distinct emission profiles were incorporated as model imaging agents and evaluated using an in vivo imaging system (IVIS). The engineered phantoms enabled quantitative assessment of wavelength-dependent fluorescence, lesion visualization and delineation across diverse geometries and tissue backgrounds, multiplexed imaging of spatially distinct lesions, and simulation of fluorescence-guided tumor resection. Constructs incorporating GFP-expressing cancer cells further demonstrated simultaneous visualization of cellular and nanoprobe-derived fluorescence. Collectively, these findings establish anatomically programmable TMPs as a versatile, reproducible framework for benchmarking fluorescent imaging agents, systematically interrogating anatomical and optical determinants of imaging performance, and advancing fluorescence-guided surgical strategies before in vivo evaluation and clinical translation.

title: Discrepancies in Interpretation of Japanese Radiology Report Expressions Between Radiologists and Referring Physicians
abstract: ObjectivesTo evaluate discrepancies between radiologists and referring physicians in the interpretation of diagnostic probabilities conveyed by common Japanese expressions used in radiology reports. Materials and MethodsFifteen expressions commonly used to convey diagnostic probabilities in radiology reports were selected by five attending radiologists. An anonymous online survey was distributed to 26 radiologists and 33 referring physicians at a single institution. Participants assigned a diagnostic probability (from 0% to 100% in 10% increments) to each expression. Differences in median probabilities between radiologists and referring physicians were analyzed using the Mann-Whitney U test. Variability in interpretation was assessed using interquartile range (IQR), with IQR [≥] 30% defined as substantial variability. ResultsAll radiologists (26/26) and 97% of referring physicians (32/33) completed the survey. Seven of the 15 expressions showed statistically significant differences in interpretation between radiologists and referring physicians: "c/w" (80% vs. 60%; p = 0.031), the Japanese equivalents of "present" (100% vs. 100%; p = 0.024), "suspect of" (80% vs. 70%; p = 0.007), "possibly" (50% vs. 70%; p < 0.001), "unlikely" (10% vs. 10%; p = 0.022), "cannot be ruled out" (25% vs. 40%; p < 0.001), and "not inconsistent with" (80% vs. 90%; p = 0.008). Substantial variability in interpretation (IQR [≥] 30%) was observed for four expressions: "cannot be ruled out" (IQR, 10%-40%), "s/o" (IQR, 60%-90%), "c/w" (IQR, 50%-90%), and "not inconsistent with" (IQR, 70%-100%). ConclusionThis study revealed that nearly half of the Japanese expressions commonly used to convey diagnostic probabilities were interpreted differently by radiologists and referring physicians. These discrepancies highlight the need for a standardized lexicon to improve clarity and consistency in radiology reporting. Compliance with Reporting GuidelinesThis study was conducted in accordance with the STROBE guidelines for observational studies.
